title: Don't grow weary (Galatians 6:1–10)
hookLine: restore gently; carry burdens; don't grow weary in doing good
carry: in due season we shall reap
tomorrow: who says a blessing over a cup of coffee, and why?

cards: Third week tutoring, and the kid still won't look up from his phone. A month of checking on a friend through her bad stretch, and she hasn't once asked about yours.
Doing good can start to feel like dropping coins down a well and never hearing them land. Paul ends Galatians writing to people in that exact spot.
And he starts somewhere unexpected: with somebody who has messed up, and everybody knows it.

teach.b: "Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." Restore, gently, with one eye on yourself.
Then: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Three verses later: "For every man shall bear his own burden." Which is it?
Here's one to tell a friend: some readers point out that Paul uses two different Greek words. The first is a crushing weight, too heavy for one back.
The second is more like the pack each person carries on a march. Help with the boulders; carry your own bag.
Then Paul turns farmer: "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap."
And the line for anyone tired of doing right with nothing to show for it: "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not." Due season. Not this afternoon.
Seeds don't report back while they're underground, and Paul doesn't promise they will. He only promises a season.
Then he widens the field: "let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith."

teach.h: IN DUE SEASON WE SHALL REAP.
teach.b: The church family first in line, but not the only ones in line.

how: Galatians 6:2 and 6:9 are lines some Christians keep close in long stretches of caregiving or volunteering; some churches organize members to share one another's practical burdens, from meals to rides.

games.q: a teammate who bailed on practice all month finally shows up, and the group chat is already roasting him. what's Paul's first move?
o: restore him gently, and remember you could slip too.
let the roast run; he earned every bit of it.
ignore him until he apologizes to the whole team.
games.why: restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted. gentle, and humble about it.

practice: Before the sit ends, do one more good thing within reach: refill someone's water, answer the message you've been putting off, put back what someone else left out. Small and unseen is fine.
Then sit, and let it be a seed you don't dig up to check on.

wordCard.voice: Don't grow weary. Paul's word to tired people at the end of Galatians: keep sowing; the harvest has its own season.

orig.note: Greek: a weight, a burden. The word behind bear ye one another's burdens.

carryVoice: Your line: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. Seeds keep working in the dark. Rest well tonight.
